title: Maresius, Wendelin, Alting: gift that fiducially applies Gospel promises
source_text: X. Samuel Maresius in Systemate, loco undecimo, fidem dicit esse Donum, quo promissionibus Evangelii in Christo, tanquam veris & certis acquiescimus, easque nobis fiducialiter applicamus. Quibus concinit Wendelinus in Academia Anhaltina Theologiae Professor notissimus, docens, fidem esse id quo electi credunt divinae veritati, & firmae voluntatis affectione promissiones gratiae salutaris in Christo accipiunt, sibique Christum cum omnibus beneficiis ejus ad vitam aeternam applicant. Christianae Theologiae lib. 1. cap. 24. Thesi 4. Nec absimilis est definitio Henrici Altingii olim in Academia Heydelbergensi Professoris, cui fides est, Cognitio gratiae Dei in Christo Redemptore, & ejusdem fiducialis apprehensio, qua quisque fidelis illam sibi singulariter applicat. Locor. commun. parte 1. pag. 117.
pass_a_gloss: Samuel Maresius in the System, place eleven, says faith is a Gift by which we rest in the promises of the Gospel in Christ as true and sure, and fiducially apply them to ourselves. With which agrees Wendelin, most noted Professor of Theology in the Anhalt Academy, teaching that faith is that by which the elect believe the divine truth, and with a firm affection of will receive the promises of saving grace in Christ, and apply to themselves Christ with all His benefits unto eternal life. Christian Theology book 1, ch. 24, Thesis 4. Nor unlike is the definition of Henry Alting, formerly Professor in the Heidelberg Academy, for whom faith is Knowledge of the grace of God in Christ the Redeemer, and a fiducial apprehension of the same, by which each of the faithful applies it to himself singularly. Common Places, part 1, p. 117.
pass_b_english: Maresius: faith = gift that rests in Gospel promises as true/sure and applies them fiducially.
Wendelin: elect believe divine truth; firm-will receive saving promises; apply Christ and all benefits.
Alting: knowledge of God’s grace in Christ the Redeemer + fiducial grasp applied to myself singularly.
